summary: This note argues that local wetlands are vital for water purification, biodiversity, carbon storage, flood control, recreation, education and the local economy. It cites several experts and dated 2023 presentations and reports to support each function. It concludes that wetlands are highly threatened by urbanization, pollution, invasive species and climate change, and calls for stronger conservation and community involvement.
one_line: Local wetlands filter water, support biodiversity, store carbon, regulate floods and add economic value, but face serious threats that call for conservation action.
key_facts: Wetlands are called the "kidneys of the landscape" because they filter water, absorbing pollutants like nitrogen, phosphorus and sediments from run-off.
Dr. Emily Carter, an ecologist from Silverwater University, described wetlands as a sponge in a seminar on September 4, 2023.
Wetland plants take up excess nutrients that could otherwise cause eutrophication and harmful algal blooms.
Dr. Raymond Briggs presented on wetland biodiversity at the Greenlands Conservation Forum on October 12, 2023, noting wetlands are among the world's most productive ecosystems.
Ornithologist Susan Zhang reported sighting the endangered blue-throated macaw on a research trip on September 15, 2023.
Dr. Oliver Hendricks said on November 7, 2023 that peatlands cover about 3% of the world's surface but hold at least a third of the soil carbon.
Wetland soils are anoxic, which slows decomposition and produces carbon-rich soils that help regulate global temperatures.
During heavy rainfall in early September 2023, local wetlands absorbed large volumes of water and prevented potentially catastrophic flooding in adjacent communities.
Hydrologist Dr. Fiona Roberts confirmed the wetlands' flood-moderating role in an assessment report dated September 21, 2023.
Wetlands recharge groundwater aquifers and store water in wet seasons to ensure supply during droughts.
Dr. Laura Kim's October 30, 2023 economic report estimated the ecosystem services of local wetlands at several million dollars annually, including non-use values.
Wetlands support fishing, eco-tourism and rice cultivation, and serve as outdoor classrooms for education.
Urbanization, pollution, invasive species and climate change threaten wetlands, and some wetlands are now protected under law.
